utterances.text: That is where we collected these women who were on the meadow near that bridge, and it was visible, by the traces of blood on the ground, that at least one or two bodies had been taken from there. And from there, I remember at least five or six bodies of women were taken, those that had not been collected already, and then we took them to where I already told you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do I understand your evidence to be that you recall a total of five or six bodies that were in the truck that you took to be buried in the bush, or were there more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, it was five or six bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at paragraphs 35 and 36. In the interests of time, I may just -- well, I'll deal with it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall an incident in the village of Rogovo, south of Orahovac, near the end of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, without too much detail: Did something happen in that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Rogovo -- well, we went there. The sergeant told us to take flour, oil, and other foodstuffs, any food that we found in the shops or in the cars, the shop vans --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or spare parts from the vans, to take some food, and when we went round the houses, that we could take flour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me interrupt you there. During the course of doing that, did you hear some shots, and did you go and find out what happened after you heard those shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you because there was an interruption in the interpretation, so I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the course of taking the things from the village, as you've indicated, did you at some point in time hear some shots being fired, and did you go and investigate as to what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, when we were entering a house, when I was in a house, across the road - and when I say "across the road," there was a macadamised road there in the village - and in the opposite house, that is to say, across the road, you could hear shots. There were shots from our own automatic weapons, and you could also hear one or two bullets fired which were different from ours. So we left the house very quickly. The two or three of us who were in the house left the house quickly and ran towards this other house, from which we heard the shooting. When we ran into the house, upstairs there were two of our soldiers, who told us that everything was all right and that there were no more -- that is to say that everything had been -- that everything was over, that we shouldn't be afraid, because the shooting was done at the shooting -- the two people who were there were shot at. So when they told us, what they said was when they entered the house, they found two people there. One was listening to a walkman and smoking a cigarette, and another one was sleeping in a corner of the room, on the floor. And when they opened the door, they shot them, and they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any explanation as to the sound of the other bullets that you said you heard that sounded different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The man who was standing inside the house had on him - what's it called? - a jacket with bullets, rifle bullets, three or four rounds with these bullets, and when our own soldiers shot at them, they hit him there, and one or two of their bullets were shot from this round when the bullet hit him --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the cartridge. So we -- that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I think we may need to look at the clock, the time the witness has had, and to allow time for cross-examination so we can finish the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I definitely want to move on relatively quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, within a week of -- I'm sorry. Just one question about that. Is it true that these men that were shot were wearing KLA uniforms or had some KLA insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was wearing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. I just want to move on, sir. Do you recall an incident where you were going to be tasked with going to the Tusus area, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were tasked to go to the -- we weren't tasked to go to the Tusus area, but it was said that the army should go to Tusus, and we discussed this. Soldiers Milosevic and Markovic said that they had had enough, they had had their fill of all these events and couldn't go on any more and carry out any more assignments. And then this reached the ears of Captain Gavrilovic, who, when he heard it, made the company line up, stand to attention in the corridor downstairs. And when he went out of his office, he said, "Where are those two experts who are demoralising the whole army?" And then he called them and said to them -- he pointed to them, "You expert Milosevic, you expert Markovic, step out of the line." And then he said, "Do you know that the death penalty exists in the army for doing things like you did? And do you know, Milosevic, that you were forgiven for not carrying out orders once?" And he took out a pistol. It was a Scorpio pistol that he had at his belt. He cocked the pistol at Private Markovic, placed it at his temple, and told them to go out, and in front of me he told the sergeants and the soldiers from the rest of the company, "Go to your assignments." He ordered them to go about their daily assignments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you leave while he was still pointing the gun at Markovic's head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was still pointing the gun at his head. And they moved towards the door that was ahead of them, in front of them, the door to the school. They walked in front, whereas we went into the classrooms that were to the left and right of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say that all of your soldiers, your company, had been gathered together to witness this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the next day, if anything, with respect to what you know to have happened to Markovic and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we know, Markovic and Milosevic were taken away to the basement, the cellar of the school building, where they were tied up and where they spent five days. At the entrance to that cellar, there was a soldier on guard, standing guard. But in the late-night hours when the sergeant wasn't there, we asked the guard to let us go down and see them. And I personally went down two or three times, down into the cellar to see them. And they were very frightened. They didn't know what was going to happen to them. And that's where they spent five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever punished or disciplined by your superiors or the army for being involved in the shooting incident in Trnje or any of the other indents in which you participated, according to your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav army, I was never disciplined for incidents of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were warned by His Honour Judge May today, and it was explained to you by me and by investigators prior to this about subjecting yourself to potential legal consequences for giving self-incriminating evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told you had the right to a lawyer, and you said you didn't want one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's clear you understood you didn't have to answer any of my questions today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why, sir, did you come forward to give your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came forward to give my evidence because I wanted in this way to express everything that is troubling me, that has been troubling me for the past three years since the time I completed my service in the army. The thing that I find most troubling is that never a night goes by without my dreaming of that child who was hit by that bullet and who was crying. And I thought that if I come forward and tell the truth that I will feel easier in my soul. And that is the only reason why I am here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you feel about your participation in these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how I feel now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I am testifying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. How do you feel about what it is you did during the period when you were in the army and the things you've testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About that period, I think that very shameful acts were committed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. I think the word was "shameful."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I deeply regret that something like that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my questions, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K41, you're now going to be asked some questions by the accused. Make sure you understand the questions before you answer them. If you don't understand them, say so. If you don't answer -- if you don't know the answer or you can't remember, say so. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as it's already a quarter to twelve, tell me, please, how much time I'm to be given for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can have the same as the Prosecution. You can have for the rest of today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me just see him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, no. All I know is that they came looking for me to my home, and my brother said they had come looking for me but that they didn't tell him why they were looking for me. But they didn't come again after that one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, K41. Do you know why a warrant for your arrest was issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I do not know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that a warrant was issued for your arrest because you committed a crime, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He knows nothing about it. He's told you. And there is absolutely no good reason for mentioning any of this, particularly in open session. If you have any further questions about this, we're going into closed session. Now, you've got his answer. He knows nothing about it. Do you want to ask him anything more?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have many questions, Mr. May, with respect to his testimony, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can go on and ask questions about other topics, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the right to question the credibility of this witness and to test it, and quite obviously we're dealing with a criminal here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to say that many of the questions so far, including numbers of alleged warrants, ought be redacted. Just that whole -- might we have that whole aspect redacted because it might tend to identify the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, on a different topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9808 to 9814.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we have established the credibility of this witness, then I can move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: K41, you were first interviewed, you were first asked about the activities of your unit at the Ljubizda Has village. That was before the NATO aggression, at the time when you provided security for that border belt, the border area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not provide security, Milosevic, for that border belt. It was our assignment, as I said. That is to say, I told you what our company's tasks were. And we were just given the task, that is to say, we were told to go and have a show of force, to demonstrate our might in the area. But this proved to be quite incorrect, because that's not what we're doing. We weren't having a show of force. We went there to do what I recounted earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K41, I know this is difficult because the accused is asking the questions. Do not reply to him. Do not call him by name. You are giving evidence to the Court, not to him. Now, would you bear that in mind, please. Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to your own testimony, you were in an ambush at the Ljubizda Has village, which on the map, map 10, number 10, was shown. And according to the scale of the map, you can see that you had set up an ambush somewhere towards the border. You said that you were in an ambush up above the village of Has. And it is just four kilometres away from the state border with Albania. So you manned that ambush. It was a legitimate ambush. Was there any kind of engagement while you were in that ambush?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, we had come from the barracks in the early morning hours. We were placed on the alert. We were told what I said. We passed through the village of Ljubizda Has and went up above the village where they told us to set up an ambush above the village and that anybody coming in or passing by, and there's the Pastrik mountain there, anybody coming down from the mountain should be shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You didn't say that you actually shot at anyone. You didn't tell us that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at that time, while we were in that ambush on that first day, we didn't shoot at anyone. In the evening, when we returned to the houses where the villagers -- from which the villagers had been expelled, when we were in the houses, the military police brought in a young man, and they had put the upper part of a KLA uniform on him and the man was shot through the leg. And during the night, when they were transporting him back to the barracks, this young man was killed. After that, the next day, while we were standing and manning the ambush above the village, a man came by wearing a civilian uniform, and the people manning the ambush started shooting at him, but the man raised his hands up in the air and he was captured and turned over to Lieutenant Colonel Konjikovac in the village of Ljubizda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. During the examination-in-chief, you said that you manned the ambush at Ljubizda Has, which means that this is up in the mountains, along the border belt towards Albania, and you said you spent the night in the houses, in the village houses, and that's what you explained. Then you went on to say how -- then you went on to describe the events in the village of Jeskovo, which was also, as far as I could see from all these facts, somewhere -- it took place around the 11th of March, 1999, from 0400 hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was in February, but I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's say it was in February. That's not the important point. K41, is it true that during the operation conducted in the village of Jeskovo, you were not able to see the bodies of ten people, but just three terrorists, which was the number of dead bodies that your commander saw? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you happen to know that this event was attended by the representatives of the Verification Mission, the OSCE Verification Mission, from its regional centre in Prizren, and that they conducted a verification spot-check on the very location? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that, because I wasn't there -- it wasn't my place to know who would come in to verify what. I was there as a soldier, and I had my own commander and I received orders which I had to carry out, and that's why I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you spoke about Jeskovo, so I'm asking you whether you know, as you are giving exhaustive details here, that nine killed terrorists were ascertained to be on the spot, wearing uniforms and carrying weapons. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as far as I know, in that operation about 30 individuals were killed. On the basis of what I saw, none of them were wearing uniforms. I didn't see anybody in uniform or with weapons belonging to an army. All I saw was a hunting rifle that one of them had, one of the people that had been taken into custody had had. That's what I heard with my own ears and saw with my own eyes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, K41. As you do not know about the Verification Mission and the verification itself, did you learn that General Maisonneuve, the head of the regional centre in Prizren, was apprised of this, as well as his associates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's no point putting that. He doesn't know. He said he was just an ordinary soldier, he didn't know about the OSCE. You can put the evidence in front of us in due course, if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, I'm asking him about something that he seems to allege in a very assertive manner, and we're talking about a legitimate ambush at Ljubizda Has and an operation at Jeskovo that was verified by the Verification Mission itself, and I have a whole list of individuals from Poland, Finland, Russia, who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. It's pointless going on like this. He doesn't know. Now, you can put the report in front of us in due course, but for the moment you're examining this witness and he's given you his evidence. Now, is there anything more you want to ask about the village?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why you're asking me that. Of course I have a large number of questions, because this witness, like many others, is a false witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put your questions and don't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the description, roughly speaking, of the events: We divided up in teams, went from house to house. I was present when Sergeant Rajko Kozlina took out a whole family from a house. There were at least 15 of them, of all ages, from babies held by their mothers up to a 70-year-old elderly man. In addition to this old man and a young boy, there were no other males. Actually, in the whole village, not a single male was found. That is approximately what you have been describing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not it, Mr. Milosevic. I did not say that Rajko Kozlina took out whole families out of houses. They were taken out by the army, by the soldiers. We soldiers took them out, Mr. Milosevic. And it is not correct what you are claiming that in the whole village there was only one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm claiming. I'm just describing the event to you according to the description given by Witness K32, because Mr. Ryneveld cautioned you at the beginning of your testimony that you have the name and surname of the witness - you said you knew him - and that you should mention him as K32 and not his name. And he testified about the very same event, didn't he? So I'm reading part of his testimony to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what he saw and heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K41, I think you were going to answer in the same way. The witness can't comment on what somebody else said. All he can talk about is his own evidence, and that's what he's told you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I'm asking, whether that is the incident. He says that they shot at the entire group, that he heard shooting, that they killed these 15 persons. He mentions a baby. So it is same incident that is described. In other words --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which village are you talking about now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I am first of all speaking about the event itself, and I wish to show that these witnesses did not reach the right kind of agreement when they were supposed to tell these falsehoods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That, Mr. Milosevic, is an allegation which should be put to the witness, and then we'll come back and clarify what it is you're asking about, because it's by no means clear. Witness K41, what the accused has alleged is that you and another witness have put your heads together to invent a false story. Now, that's the allegation made by the accused. Is there any truth in it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a pure falsehood. I am just talking about what I saw and what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now we'll go back to the cross-examination. Now, which village are you asking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may I clarify this once again, please? Is what K32 claims true, after this other event that you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. You are confusing everybody. I don't know whether you're doing it deliberately or not. I have asked you a simple question. You have refused to answer. Now, if you want to continue with this cross-examination, you must do so in a way which is clear and fair to the witness and also clear to the Court. Now, which village are you asking questions about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm asking about the event, because both of them are talking about the same event. For example, K32 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It doesn't matter about K32. You're being asked a straightforward question to clarify your examination for the Court, and the Court has a right to be told, and the witness, what you're asking about. You see, I suspect that you're trying to confuse him by going from village to village, particularly when you refer to the 15 people who were killed. Now, it's a matter for you. If you want to continue this cross-examination, you must tell us which village and tell the witness which village you're asking about. Are you asking about Trnje?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you, Mr. May. I will tell you and the witness and all of those who are watching this. An identical event, an identical story, is recounted by K32 and K41, except that K32 refers to the village of Medvedje, and this witness refers to this same event as an event taking place in Trnje. Please, take a look at this. You have it on page 03 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, you can make these points to us. You can argue all this in due course, but this isn't a matter for this witness. This witness has given his account. He's told you what he says happened in Trnje, that he saw and heard and participated in. Now, that's his evidence. Now, that's what you can ask him about. You can't ask him about what some other witness said. If you say there were discrepancies between them, you can point that out to us. Now, you were asking about Jeskovo, but I understand now you're going on to Trnje. Ask the witness some questions about what he saw or heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When, as you say, Captain Gavrilovic ordered you to collect all the women's and children's bodies - however, the bodies of the children and of most of the women were not there - you collected the bodies of five persons and boarded them onto the truck; is that right? Is that what you were saying a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in Trnje, in the yard where those 15 or so persons were killed, as far as I can remember - I think it is about 15 persons - in that yard there was no one. None of them were there. However, there was visible blood in the places where they had been. And it is correct that only five or six women were collected, and one or two bodies were taken from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On the orders of Captain Gavrilovic, you went and collected that. Well, now I'm asking you to comment upon the following: K32 says the same thing; however, he says that this is the village of Medvedje. Was this in the village of Medvedje or the village of Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the village of Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This is what I have been speaking about. All right. Let's not debate the issue any further, because obviously the same event, or rather, the same story, could not be told about two villages. But let's move on. You said that Captain Gavrilovic came to the Logistics Battalion on the 23rd and announced an action in the evening. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is that he came in the evening, during the night, when the NATO bombing started, at 9.00 or 10.00. He came to the Logistics Battalion and he ordered that soldiers be issued with ammunition and everything else that is necessary, and that on the next day we would be going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct, since you were the Logistics Battalion, that actually you did not even participate in some combat operations; rather, you supplied the army with food, water, and everything else they needed, and that on this occasion you were only charged -- you were only in charge of blocking that hill above the village of Trnje? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, from the month of December -- as I mentioned, from the month of December we started going into these actions that I referred to before. This was no longer the Logistics Battalion that only provides logistical support. It is not only duties that the Technical Company is supposed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right, K41. Is it correct that at that place you spent -- or rather, this was 500 or 600 metres away from the village of Trnje, that in front of you there were fields, that it was foggy, that you spent four or five days in that place, and that during that time the unit only carried out this blockade, without engaging in any movement or combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I described the event in detail a few minutes ago when the Prosecutor was putting questions to me. Do I have to repeat all of the same things as well, why we were there, what the orders were, and what we were doing there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: K41, I know it's difficult to be cross-examined and challenged in this way, but the accused is entitled to ask you some questions about your evidence, and provided they're proper questions, would you try and answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. K41, I have here a statement of then Captain First Class Major Pavle Gavrilovic in which he says: "Every member of the battalion bore in mind a reminder of the rules of conduct for fighters that I got from the superior command which clearly establishes how wounded -- how the wounded and how prisoners of war and civilians should be treated and which provides basic rules for behaviour in combat as well as basic humanitarian law. We do not have any information to the effect that any of the members of the unit that I commanded behaved contrary to the mentioned rule." Is that true or is that not true, Witness K41?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is not true. That is what all the soldiers from the Logistics Battalion know, not only me. And none of us had this handbook that you're referring to, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I have here an order of the commander of the 549th Brigade signed and stamped by Colonel Bozidar Delic. It's a three-page document dated the 4th of February, 1999. It had to have been read out to you, the order of the commander of the brigade. Under item 12 of that order issued by Colonel Delic it says -- please pay attention to this and tell me whether you remember that this order was read out to you. The order is from the 4th of February, 1999. Point 12 says: "The entire brigade should be informed about the military political situations, the intentions and the objectives of the NATO forces and the Siptar units and the possible effects of enemy moral and political efforts should be made known to all."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot follow the pace of the reading. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Slow down in the reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is whether he is aware of the order. And I'm just reading one item. "The entire brigade should be made aware of the provisions. Geneva Convention and treatment of prisoners and wounded from the enemy forces. The deadline is the 8th of February, 1999. This is an ongoing assignment, a permanent assignment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you made aware of that, K41?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am not aware of that nor was this ever read. I never heard about that while I was in Prizren in the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Since in this order is the deployment of units, the mainstays, et cetera, including this particular item that is highlighted, I think that it should be exhibited here, that it should become part of the evidence, unless you refuse that as well. But I do have other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You can hand in the document. It will be marked for identification, and if there's no dispute about it, it will be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A short while ago I read a brief quotation to you from the statement of Major Pavle Gavrilovic, who was then a captain first class and commander. You said that that is not correct, what he said, that is. You have the statement of Nedeljkovic, sergeant first class. I'm not going to read it out to you, not all of it. He says only the following: "The unit was commanded by Pavle Gavrilovic, Captain First Class, and he issued clear orders to us in cutting off the channels of communication and behaving towards prisoners and civilians, and each and every one of us had 'Rules for Combatants.' The group of soldiers that I commanded did not carry out any movements and did not enter any built-up areas. I personally did not hear of anyone from my unit not respecting the 'Rules for Combatants' that we got from the superior command." So your commander, Sergeant First Class Milan Nedeljkovic, says that you did not carry out any movements and that you did not enter built-up areas at all. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's one matter first of all. As I understand it, the commander was, in fact, Kozlina and not the man you're mentioning. Is that right, K41?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Nedeljkovic was commander for the Quatermasters Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was he your superior officer in this company as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commanding officer for his platoon. And in my platoon it was my own sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I also have the statement of Muhamed Fejzic. You call him Miroslav Fejzic. He's not Miroslav. It is Muhamed Fejzic, Senior Sergeant. You also mentioned him. He says: "None of us went or -- went to or enter the village of Mamusa." And he explains that the direction of movement was Prizren, Ljubizda, Novake and the ultimate objective, the vineyards above the village of Novake or, rather, the hill above Trnje. We saw on the map that this hill is between the villages of Novake and Trnje. And these officers from your company say that you kept that hill under blockade, that you were not engaged in combat, and that you did not enter built-up areas. Muhamed Fejzic says here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- no one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You must allow the witness to deal with these matters. Witness K41, what is now alleged is that you kept a hill under blockade, you were not engaged in combat, and you didn't enter built-up areas. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain this to you, Your Honour. I did explain it awhile ago as well. When we arrived at that hill, Sergeant Fejzic remained there with his soldiers on that hill. And Sergeant Nedeljkovic and Sergeant Kozlina set out to Trnje, the village of Trnje. That's the truth. And that is how the situation evolved on the ground where I was. Mr. Milosevic, what you have written down there is something that I'm not going to go into. I'm just saying what I saw and what I heard about where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Senior Sergeant Muhamed Fejzic says further on: "During 1998 and 1999, in the midst of the most pronounced actions by the Siptar forces, each and every one of the soldiers was cautioned by Colonel Delic and his associates as well as the commanding officers of the units to respect the human rights and all other rights of all the inhabitants within the area of responsibility of the commander of the brigade regardless of where the unit was." Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you did not even meet or, rather, you did not even clash with the KLA, that did you not see them, that you were not engaged in any combat, that you were just going and killing babies, women, and children. Please show on the ELMO this KFOR confidential. You see "K Brigade location." This was drawn up immediately after the war, and it shows the area of responsibility of this brigade where K41 was. Each and every one of these flags depicts a brigade, and this is a list of locations and a list of all brigades in those seven zones that I tried to prove here that they exist, that the KLA did have them. And this is a KFOR document showing -- you see "K Brigade locations," just so that you would see how many brigade there were and where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pass it to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution can have a look at this during the adjournment which we will take now. Witness K41, we're going to adjourn again for 20 minutes. When we come back, we'll deal with this question. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just before we continue, if I may, there's one thing that I'm not going to re-examine upon, but I think, for the record, we should put -- the accused has put to this witness about K32's reference to a different community. I just want to bring the Court's attention to paragraph 14 of the summary of K32, where he corrected his original statement, and also at page 8237, he refers to the village of Trnje. So -- and the accused had that evidence, and I just -- in fairness to the present witness, I want to bring that to the accused's attention as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To clarify, the page number is 8236 where Trnje appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm also looking at page 8237, in chief, at line 8, but this may be a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the same thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And paragraph 14 of the summary, it's also pointed out that there was a corrected statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Inquiries are being made to see whether we can sit a bit later this afternoon to finish this witness. Meanwhile, Mr. Milosevic, you wanted a document put on the ELMO. Can you see that, K41? Obviously not. See if we can have some arrangement made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told that the witness can see it, but it's difficult to read. Mr. Milosevic, perhaps you'd like to ask the witness the question that you want about that document, and we'll see if we can get anywhere with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: K41, as we were saying, do you know what the concentration of forces of the KLA was precisely in the area of responsibility of your particular brigade? Yes or no. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many soldiers from your own brigade died in the fighting with the KLA terrorist forces during the time you were in the brigade, in that Logistics Battalion, in the rear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many soldiers were killed from the brigade. I don't know that. I do know that from the Logistics Battalion, in all the fighting with the KLA, there were no losses, no losses to soldiers belonging to our battalion, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as regards the Logistics Battalion, the Logistics Battalion wasn't engaged in the fighting, so there were no persons killed. But other battalions were not rear-line battalions. What I'm asking you is the brigade, about the brigade, because you worked with the entire brigade. The Logistics Battalion did its job and work catering to the entire brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the brigade is concerned, I don't know about any casualties. All I can tell you is about my particular battalion. That's what I know about. And I know that when we would engage in these operations, there were no casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. May, as Mr. Ryneveld objected when I mentioned a detail in connection with this witness - and that is his right. He has right to do so, of course, because he is protecting the identity of his witness - could you just -- could we move into private session for just one moment for me to show you that the witness has not been telling the truth about other matters either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we have got the courtroom for longer this afternoon. If you want to play the tape, you can play it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would take up too much time, so I'm just going to ask something. And I will to tender the tape. I'll hand it in to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was precisely in the area of the village of Trnje that your brigade, together with the villagers, in the autumn of 1998 after the defeat of the KLA, built roads to help the population and that they were Albanian villages principally and that they were helped out by the Engineering Battalion, by the mechanised equipment, and some of the soldiers can be seen working alongside the Albanians from the villages building those roads? And we have statements to the effect that the army was helping them and that they were cooperating very well. Do you remember that autumn of 1998 and those works that were going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the autumn of 1998, we were building roads but roads that led to watchtowers, the border huts. And the Albanians helped us in this construction work. Whether they came of their own free will or were made to do so, I don't know, but they would bring in their tractors to help us transport the sand that we needed to cover the road surfaces with. That's all I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that in the operation that I just mentioned -- in the operation I mentioned, the one that was verified by the OSCE verifications, that not a single civilian lost their lives in the fighting around Leskovo? Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim that the ten that I saw were people wearing civilian uniforms. As to the rest, I can't say anything because I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the tape we have the village of Leskovo where a large number of weapons and ammunition was seized. And the third contribution on that tape, the third section of the tape, relates to this: You claim that you set fire to houses in Mamusa and that not a single house in Mamusa was set fire to either by our own forces or by the KLA forces, as far as my records show. And on the tape, I have statements by the inhabitants of the village of Mamusa when the police arrived in Mamusa village and liberated them from the terror that was exerted over them by members of the KLA and asked them for 500 marks for each truck to enter and 300 marks for cars to boot and that it was much easier for them once the police force had arrived. And they asked the police force to patrol in Mamusa more frequently so as not to be exposed to KLA terror of that kind. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I know about is that when we arrived, when we came to within 400 to 500 metres of the body -- of the village that they told us was called Mamusa, the first seven to eight houses which were in this periphery were shelled by an anti-aircraft gun and were later on set fire to. That's what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, K4. You said this the anti-aircraft gun that you call a three-barrelled gun, it is the Bertov [As interpreted] 20 -- millimetres. It is that kind of three-barrelled weapon. That it opened fire for some 20 minutes you said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately 20 minutes. This went on in the village for about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, K41, that the speed of fire of that gun is 2.100 shells per minute, which means 800 -- to all intents and purposes, 800 shells per minute. Are you clear on the fact that they would have needed 1.6000 shells if they had fired for 20 minutes and if what you were saying were correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you don't seem to know that there was individual gunfire there apart from this anti-aircraft gun. And this anti-aircraft gun can individually target targets or houses with one, two, or three bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And if the shooting went on for 20 minutes, then it means that it fired in the way it was capable of doing so, technically speaking. So how was this gun -- how did the shooting of this gun take place when it fired individually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say how it shot individually, but I do know that it used individual shots to target the village, Mr. Milosevic, because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How many shells would that be then fired by that gun in those 20 minutes when it was sporadically firing individual gunshots? How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps -- well, I can't really say. I don't know. I'm not quite sure how many. I can't calculate all this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that the villagers from the village of Trnje went on foot towards the village of Lesane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The village of Lesane was behind your back. So how come you let one lot go out and leave and you killed another lot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. That's not correct. The villagers who were fleeing fled to the right of us taking the road and to the left of us taking the creek. That is what is correct. And they didn't go to the rear behind us because they would have gone in the direction of the village of Novake had they done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So they fled to the right of you. Let me repeat my question. How come you let one lot flee and not another lot? You killed the other lot, whereas you let one lot go free.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, people were fleeing, hiding behind houses. Do you know what it looks like? Do you know what the configuration of the terrain is like? Of course you don't. You don't know the lie of the land. But those of us who were there know what it was like. And once they get behind a house, you're no longer able to see them going to Lesane and the creek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you entered the houses and that you would then set fire to them afterwards. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did enter the houses and the houses were set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, who issued the orders to burn the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders were issued by the sergeant who was with us. He indicated the exact house that each of us were to torch when he was able to point them out to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say in your statement that Kozlina gathered together your company, Kozlina his company, et cetera, and the other two their own. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how were they able to gather together their companies when they were just commanders of squads, not even commanders of platoons but squad commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained that, and I said that once the order had been issued by Pavle Gavrilovic, Sergeant Kozlina turned towards us and told us to rally our ranks. And after that, the members of our company gathered together, and he led the way and we carried on after him down towards Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you said that your -- that about 80 people, 80 soldiers, took part in that operation launched by your battalion. Now, can you imagine three companies with only 80 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. What's to be challenged there? I don't understand what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you know that one company does not only have 80 soldiers but many more men. And you said that they collected together three companies so that there were 80 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you know that many soldiers from our companies were manning the watchtowers? They were on assignment and their posts at the watchtowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know this: that a unit under a blockade or in a blockade like yours was not given the assignment of drawing closer to Mamusa and that there was fighting in the Brestovac, Velika Krusa, Retimlje, Opterusa, Studencani, Mamusa region until the afternoon of the 27th of March, 1999? Are you aware of that? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. Because as I have already stated -- I don't want to repeat myself and explain again what happened, you have it -- you have the description in my statement. And that's how it was, as I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you say -- you say you saw a tank and a Praga. On what date was this? When did you see the tank and the Praga?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw it -- the date was -- that night. I can't remember the exact date, but on the night that the NATO bombing started. This was on the next day, in the morning, when we went past Trnje and arrived at the bridge and when we left Trnje. That's when you could see it, on the northern hillside, a tank and a Praga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that we have, before the 27th, that is to say before the fighting ceased, from your positions you were not able to see any tanks at all because above the village of Neprebiste on the hills surrounding the village that they appeared, and that's when they were visible from the village of Trnje, only after the 27th. So perhaps you got that wrong.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes, whereas what you heard, perhaps they gave you the wrong information and the wrong facts. Perhaps that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I shall be tendering the tape with the three excerpts on it. And now I should like to move on. Let me ask you this. I'm not quite clear. Did you just set fire to the houses where you saw the curtains moving at the windows which indicated that there was someone in the house or did you take the houses in order one by one and set fire to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The houses were burnt in order, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. What were you saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The houses were burnt one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you want -- are you saying that you burnt the houses in Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have told you quite specifically that on the periphery of Mamusa eight houses were burnt which were targeted by the anti-aircraft gun first and they were torched later. So those were the only houses that were burnt. So when I say "we," we soldiers who were there later on with our soldier -- with our sergeant returned to where our company had put up. So you needn't say that that was in Mamusa because it wasn't. It was in the village of Trnje this burning one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that up until the 25th of March, in the village of Trnje, there were no soldiers and no police either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you comment as to why a soldier from your company said that you were deployed in positions around Trnje on the 4th of April? Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we were deployed on the morning after the NATO bombing began, so at dawn the next morning. We reached the reaches of the hills above the village. That's when we arrived. I can't tell you the exact date. I don't want to guess. But I do know that it was on that particular night and at dawn the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 3, paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that you took position up at the hill but outside the line of vision of the village. That's what you say. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took up our positions on the hill, and an anti-aircraft gun was positioned there, and he could see the village as if it was in the palm of your hand and he was able to be effective from there, whereas the trucks that we arrived in were placed behind the hill so that they would be out of sight of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How were you able to see -- you say that you were outside of the line of vision of the village. How were you able to target the village if you weren't able to see it, if you weren't in that line of sight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've already explained that to you. We were not outside the line of sight of the village. We were in sight of the village. We were on the hill above the village and positioned the anti-aircraft weapon up there on the hill so that it could target the village. I didn't position the anti-aircraft weapon; the soldiers in charge of it did. We were there, but we just took the trucks out of sight. It wasn't that we were out of sight; the trucks were placed out of sight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). The shelling of the village, as you say, from the anti-aircraft weapon, did it begin before or after that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling started afterwards, while we were taking up our positions in the outskirts of the village. That's when the man was killed, the man you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was it then that you noticed that some people were leaving the village and fleeing towards the Lesane village area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only when the anti-aircraft gun began to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So when the gun began to fire, you noticed that people were fleeing in the direction of the village of Lesane; is that it? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The people were trying to escape, and we could see two or three people at a time fleeing down in between the houses, and from where I was standing, I saw that they were escaping towards Lesane and towards the creek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you open fire on them? Did you shoot at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not shoot at them until the shelling went on. It was only when the shelling ceased and when we started cleaning up the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come you didn't shoot at them if you were given orders to kill them all? How can you explain that, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained that in the following way: That was what I had seen. Had I not been ordered to shoot, I would never have shot at civilians. So it was the people that I saw fleeing myself. Perhaps some other soldiers saw them. Perhaps the commanding officer did not see these people fleeing because of the configuration of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have represented this sergeant, Sergeant Kozlina, like a beast, going around killing anything in sight, and you said that the four or five of you stayed with him, as you were told to do, as he told you to do. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So which soldiers stayed with you? Give us their names, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained, Sergeant Kozlina remained behind, then there was Private Markovic and two other soldiers whose names I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about this witness K32? Did he stay behind with you as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him. I do not remember having seen him at that time, and I don't think he was there. I don't think he was in the group that remained behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to what you say, he wasn't with you. Now, tell us the first name and last name of the soldier whom you say, on page 4, paragraph 6, broke the windows of a house and then proceeded to throw a hand grenade into the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that, because us soldiers had some caps on. Others had some shields. And once two companies had gathered together at a distance of 50 metres. I was not able to see which soldiers were there exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So if you didn't see that, you can't tell us. Now, tell me this: How many houses did you personally set fire to in Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately. Give us a rough estimation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three houses perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: How many houses does the village of Trnje comprise, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly because -- I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you were able to see whether it was a big village or a small village, whether it comprised of 5 houses, 50 houses, or 500 houses. So give us a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a hundred houses, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, a hundred houses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying this, although I'm not quite certain, but 50, a hundred. That's what I seem to remember. I was just there once in that village of Trnje, on that particular occasion and never again, and it's been three and a half years since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I remember correctly? On page 5, paragraph 3, you state that Lieutenant Jacimovic, when you saw a group of people on the other side of the creek, women and children, that you were told to let them go, whereas he kept back several men. Is that what you state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Lieutenant Jacimovic only asked that these people be allowed to leave, the women and children. Now, who issued the orders, I didn't hear. I didn't hear who issued the orders for these five men to be kept behind. All he said was that the women and children should be allowed to leave. And there was an invalid amongst them, a crippled man, that I remember being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How come now Jacimovic is issuing orders all of a sudden, whereas you previously state that all the orders were issued by Sergeant Kozlina? Who was in command, in actual fact? Was it Jacimovic, Kozlina, a sergeant in command of Jacimovic who was a high-ranking officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning I explained that to you very nicely in my statement. During the actions, it was Sergeant Kozlina who took over command, and Lieutenant Jacimovic was a figurehead there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the lieutenant was asking the sergeant to let the people go?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you give us that answer again, please, Witness K41?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was. It may sound illogical, but that's the way it was, that the lieutenant did -- well, I explained to you that during the actions, it was the sergeant who took over command, because he was sort of a heroic figure, brave, courageous, and the other one was less prepared for things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me precisely: Where did you take part in the collection of bodies and their burial? In which village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is what you said when you said that you collected five or six, and you don't know whether it was five or six; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that before you, somebody else had already collected some bodies. Does that mean that you knew in advance the number of bodies that you would find there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of bodies? I don't know whether it was known exactly how many would be found, but we went to look around the village, like in that yard, the bodies of the persons who had been killed. But when we went there, there were visible traces, blood traces, on the ground, but there were no bodies. And as far as I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that you buried the bodies in some bushes in the mountains, et cetera. How many soldiers together with you participated in this which you claim happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers who collected the bodies, loaded them, and dug that grave for these persons, where they were to be buried, that is, there were about ten of us soldiers who took part in this, and there were other soldiers who came along and who provided security down on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give the names of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you their names; however, they were soldiers from Montenegro. All the soldiers who were from Montenegro were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As a soldier, do you know the rules of service of the army of Yugoslavia? You say that you completed your training and that after training you were stationed in this brigade. Are you aware of the rules of service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that according to the rules of service, in addition to these orders that I quoted to you, or showed you, you are duty-bound that even if you do get an order to carry out a crime, to commit a crime, that you are duty-bound to refuse to do so and to report that to a superior command? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's not true? It's not true that that's what it says in the rules of service, or is it not true that you did report this or did not report this? What is not the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Now I'm going to explain it to you. Probably in the rules of service that is what it says, and I'm not denying that, because I don't know whether it is what the rules of service say or do not say. However, I just know what was ordered, what we were ordered to do, and there was nothing like that in the orders we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you claim that you did not know of a single order, even of the rules of service, that you are duty-bound, in respect of an order that contains the commission of a crime, that you are duty-bound to report that to a superior command. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand what you said. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you report the commission of any one of these crimes that were allegedly committed and that you also took part in, that you also committed? Did you report that to a superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, how could we report that to anyone? To report it to the one who ordered you to do that: Is that who we were supposed to report this to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was the sergeant who ordered you to commit that, so you could have reported this to the commander of the battalion or the commander of the brigade, or some other superior commander. Is that correct or is that not correct, K41?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. And how can I report this to the commander of the battalion when he issued the order that we heard, most of the soldiers did, the one that he issued on the hill above the order [as interpreted]? And how do you think that I can report that to him, when he issued that order to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who ordered the killing of these people who had allegedly been killed? You claim that Sergeant Kozlina ordered this. Now you say that you were ordered to do so by the commander of the battalion. Who issued the order: the commander of the battalion or Sergeant Kozlina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was given orders by Sergeant Kozlina. Let that be clear. And the command that we heard before that, we heard it from our commander of the battalion for the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it perhaps correct, K41, that not a single one of them ordered you to kill civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, because I heard this, and this could also have been heard by at least ten soldiers from my company who can confirm this. And in no way can you deny that over here, because I was there, I heard that, and I saw that. And you, Mr. Milosevic, as the supreme commander, you could have come down there a bit and to see what it was like for us, and you were issuing these shameful orders to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. K41. Who questioned you from amongst the investigators of the Tribunal, this institution over here? Which investigator did you give a statement to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give an answer to you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that perhaps investigator John Zdrilic? Let me jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the same investigator worked on the statement of your colleague, witness K32?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't even know who it was, so he can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know the names of soldiers, for example, Gasparic Slobodan, Jovanovic Bojan, Mirko Vladimir, not to mention all of them now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those names seems familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these are soldiers who lost their lives precisely in the fighting with terrorist groups, Albanian terrorist groups, in the actions that you described as the killing of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the actions that I participated in, and the soldiers who went with me in these actions, there were no persons wounded and no persons killed. As for the actions that I did not participate in, I cannot make any claims, because I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, K41. Since you committed this grave crime, were you given any promises for this testimony of yours that you are giving here today before this institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am here of my own free will, and I said that before. Mr. Milosevic, when I tell this truth to the person who, in my opinion, is the most responsible for all these crimes, that already makes me feel better. I need no further promises. That is sufficient for me. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you testified about the crimes that you committed personally, you are not a fugitive from this institution, because you cooperate with it. Why are you then a fugitive? Why are you a fugitive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a fugitive, Mr. Milosevic. I am just waiting. I'm just waiting for help from my relatives to prove that it's not me. Never in my life was I ever convicted or was I brought before a court of law. Mr. Milosevic, I'm just waiting for my relatives' help to assist me in proving that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that that is supposed to be proven before judiciary authorities on whose orders a warrant for your arrest was issued, not before your relatives were supposed to prove that you did not commit this armed robbery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if I did something, I am going to be accountable and to answer before my own court of law and my own judiciary system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you intend to give yourself in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Witness K41, counsel -- the amicus, as he's called, the friend of the Court, is going to ask you a few questions. Mr. Tapuskovic, we wish not to be too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I'll have to try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness K41, is it correct that persons in our country against whom criminal proceedings are initiated cannot obtain a passport and that is the reason why you do not have this passport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You stated at the beginning of your statement that you do not have a passport; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't have a passport. I never asked for one and never had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you -- did you ask for it during the past several days in order to come to The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask for it for the already mentioned reasons, and I already told you why I did not ask for one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not go to the police when you found out that the police were looking for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I never had any problems with them, and I was never convicted, and I do not know what this is all about, that is why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely. That is why you should have gone. If you were not held accountable for anything, why did you not go to the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is why I'm going to go to the police when it suits me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you are not at home now either, where you live otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you about your statement. Everything that you said today, you said a lot of that earlier, but in this previous statement of yours, there is no mention of this burial. There is no mention of what you said happened in the village of Rogovo, Tusus, about the arrest of those soldiers. Did you say that to the investigator that you talked to when you drew up this statement of yours before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, and all of that is correct. I stand behind each and every word that I said there. And I am ready to answer every question that you put. I'm prepared to give answers to you and to everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, but that is not contained in your written statement. I would like to ask you one more thing in relation to your statement. Hello?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here in your statement it is mentioned, and so that means it is no longer true, that the event that was described here and that you already talked about occurred on the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it was on the 24th of March then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K41 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly about this event that it occurred that night when the NATO bombing started. And I'm not sure of the exact date between these two days, but it was exactly that night and that morning at dawn what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
